structure.title: Inferno · A descent among finished stories
structure.text: Lost in a wood, Dante accepts Virgil's guidance. The souls below retain their memories and powers of persuasion, although their destinations are settled. Listening sympathetically can be the pilgrim's first mistake or the beginning of a better question.

structure.title: Purgatorio · People who can still change
structure.text: On the mountain the climb takes time, sleep and the help of strangers. Souls willingly undertake painful work because their desires can be educated. Conversation between the living and the dead acquires a new practical use when a prayer can help somebody.

structure.title: Paradiso · Learning to see
structure.text: Guided by Beatrice through the heavens, Dante keeps seeing what his eyes can bear and then learning why that appearance needs correction. Questions about justice, love and the limits of sight become urgent for a traveller trying to put the experience into words afterwards.

people.name: Dante
people.text: The frightened man in the scene has not yet learned what the poet telling it knows. Sometimes a speech moves him very strongly just where its speaker would most like to move him.

people.name: Virgil
people.text: Dante loves his poetry before meeting him. Virgil can command, comfort and interpret, yet belongs to a world before Christianity. His care for the traveller gradually makes the limits of his own journey painful.

people.name: Beatrice
people.text: She has taken an interest in the journey long before Dante can see her. Her teaching may involve a searching question or a rebuke. Being loved by her gives him considerable work to do.

context.title: A medieval Italian city in the afterlife
context.text: Local feuds, families, clerics and exiles share space with heroes of antiquity. Many strangers first want to know where Dante comes from. The passions of a Florentine street can survive the body's death with surprising strength.

context.title: Why the dead ask for something
context.text: The living traveller can carry a name back, correct a story, ask relatives to pray. Each speaker has reasons to select what Dante should know. A moving account can be incomplete in a way that matters.

notice.text: Listen for changes in the soundscape.
notice.why: Cries and colliding voices give way on the mountain to groups singing together. How people can share a sound tells us something about what they can still share with one another.

notice.text: Where does the guide look when the pilgrim looks at a soul?
notice.why: The face of a teacher can offer a second reading of an encounter. At other moments the pilgrim must formulate a question before the guide will give him what he needs.

notice.text: Watch what happens to an earthly comparison.
notice.why: A bird feeding its young or a worker looking up from a task can give a reader a foothold in unfamiliar territory. The more extraordinary the vision, the more precious these remembered gestures become.

opening: Lost in a dark wood, Dante finds that the way out leads through the dead. There he meets lovers, politicians, teachers, and enemies, each fixed in a condition that reveals what governed their lives. Some speak so beautifully that their punishment feels unbearable; others would prefer to keep their story off the record. Dante puts his own world on trial while travelling through it as a frightened, curious man who keeps discovering that sympathy and judgment do not reliably point in the same direction.
